newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN JEWISH RESTITUTION GROUP TO GO PUBLIC.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN JEWISH RESTITUTION GROUP TO GO PUBLIC.

text.p: The Belgian branch of the World Jewish Restitution Organisation, taking part in efforts to get back money, gold and valuables stolen from Jews during World War Two, will hold a public conference for the first time on Sunday.

"Certain things are starting to happen. There have been the revelations from the American and British archives and people are starting to ask what we are doing," a spokeswoman for the Coordination Committee for Jewish Organisations in Belgium told Reuters on Thursday.
"It is a meeting to set the record straight. But as this is the first time we have held such a public meeting I am certain there will be some important declarations," she added.
The conference will start at 7.45 p.m. (1845 GMT) on Sunday, February 23 in the Espace Yitzhak Rabin, 52, Rue Hotel des Monnaies, Brussels.

Apart from representatives of the numerous secular and religious Jewish organisations in Belgium, Greville Janner, British parliamentarian and member of the Board of Jewish Deputies, and Henri Hajdenberg, chairman of the Representative Council of French Jewish Institutions, will also take part.

Switzerland in particular has been in the headlines following revelations from the British and American wartime archives that it unashamedly profited from Jewish gold looted by Hitler's Nazis during World War Two.
Swiss citizens have been accused of buying the stolen gold, and banks of storing it and failing to hand it back to its rightful owners -- or their survivors -- after the war.
The Swiss government said on Wednesday it believed a fund for victims of the Holocaust could be set up by the end of the month using 100 million Swiss francs ($68 million) given by the banks.
An international panel of historians was also created in December to examine all the evidence against the Swiss and their banks.

Its first task is to draw up a record of Swiss purchases of looted gold from Nazi Germany and look at Switzerland's wartime immigration policy that excluded 30,000 refugees, most of whom were Jewish -- during the Nazi extermination campaign.
